# **How did the Cincinnati Reds do in the 2026 regular season?**

How many games did they play, how many did they win, and when did they play them? You'll make a request, turn what comes back into a table, and then check whether the table says what you think it says.

A few things:

1.  Add `#| echo: false` to your code blocks.
2.  Use a new block when you move to a new task.
3.  Code goes in the blocks. **Answers go outside them**, as prose. A comment inside a code chunk is not an answer.
4.  Save the raw response to a file **once**, then work from the file. You'll see why in Part 1.

Due Monday at 8pm.

# Part 1: Ask

## The request

These parameters will get you the Reds' 2026 regular season:

| parameter  | value  | meaning               |
|------------|--------|-----------------------|
| `sportId`  | `1`    | Major League Baseball |
| `teamId`   | `113`  | Cincinnati Reds       |
| `season`   | `2026` |                       |
| `gameType` | `R`    | regular season        |

Build the request, send it, and check the status.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

library(tidyverse)
library(httr2)

request <- request("https://statsapi.mlb.com/api/v1/schedule?sportId=1&teamId=113&season=2026&gameType=R")

request <- request |>
  req_perform()

raw_request <- resp_body_string(request)

resp_status(request)
```

## Read the fine print

The first field in every response is `copyright`.

```{r}
#| warning: false

```

> What does it say? Follow the link it gives you. What kinds of use does MLB permit?
>
> The first URL says "Copyright 2026 MLB Advanced Media, L.P. Use of any content on this page acknowledges agreement to the terms posted here <http://gdx.mlb.com/components/copyright.txt>"
>
> The second link that is the statement above takes you to a site stating that the use of this material is only for Individual, non-commercial, and non-bulk use.

> Is this assignment a permitted use? Would it still be if all 25 of us wrote a loop that requested every game of every season? Explain.
>
> Yes, we are permitted to use this material because we are using it for our individual uses for this assignment. No it would not be permitted, after the 25 of us use it to request every game of the season, then it would not be considered bulk use.

## Save it, then work from the file

Save the raw response to `data/raw/reds_2026.json`. Then read it back in with `jsonlite::read_json()` and use **that** for the rest of the assignment. Put the saving and the reading in **separate** blocks. Once the file is saved, add `#| eval: false` to every block that sends a request **and** to the block that saves, so rendering reads your file instead of asking MLB again.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
#| eval: false

library(jsonlite)


writeLines(raw_request,"data/raw/reds_2026.json")


mlb_data <- jsonlite::read_json("data/raw/reds_2026.json")

```

> Why work from the file instead of sending the request every time you render? Give two reasons. It renders faster because it isn't waiting on the API. The results are the same every time, incase the API updates then we still have the same results to use.

> Fill this in:
>
> - URL: [https://statsapi.mlb.com/api/v1/schedulesportId=1&teamId=113&season=2026&gameType=R](https://statsapi.mlb.com/api/v1/schedule?sportId=1&teamId=113&season=2026&gameType=R)
> - Date and time requested: Sunday Oct. 18th, 4:06 pm
> - Status: 200

> If you ran this same request in March 2027, would you get exactly the same file? What might change?
>
> The data might change, if they update the API for the games in 2027.

# Part 2: Make it a table

## Look before you reshape

Use `str()` the way we did in class: look at one date, then one game inside it.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

str(mlb_data$dates[[1]], max.level = 4)

```

> Which parts are `[ ]` (lists of things, which become rows) and which are `{ }` (named things, which become columns)? Write the path from the top of the response down to the Reds' score in one game.
>
> Dates and games are \[ \] and all else is a { }. The path from top to the reds score in one game is dates, games, home or away, and score.

## Rectangle it

Create a tibble called `reds` with **one row per entry in `games`** and these columns:

- `game_pk` (`gamePk`)
- `game_date` (`gameDate`)
- `official_date` (`officialDate`)
- `status` (`status` to `detailedState`)
- `home_id`, `away_id` (the team ids)
- `home_score`, `away_score`

Start from `tibble(day = sched$dates)`. In class, `features` was one list of earthquakes. Here, games are a list **inside** a list of dates. How many times will you need `unnest_longer()`? Once you're at one row per game, `hoist()` works the way it did in class.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

mlb_tbl <- tibble(day = mlb_data$dates) |> 
  unnest_longer(day) |> 
  unnest_wider(day, names_sep = "") |> 
  unnest_longer(games)


```

> How many rows does `reds` have? What does `totalGames` say?

> A Major League regular season is 162 games. What's going on?

> **If your raw response is a character string (text):** Use `writeLines(raw_response, "data/raw/reds_2026.json")` directly without `toJSON()`.
>
> Then I kept getting an error in this "Error in writeLines(request, "data/raw/reds_2026.json") : can only write character objects" so i added that into the google AI that was being used and it gave me this.
>
> library(httr2)
>
> # Ensure the folder exists
>
> dir.create("data/raw", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
>
> # Extract the text and write it
>
> raw_text \<- resp_body_string(request) writeLines(raw_text, "data/raw/reds_2026.json")
